title: Supreme Court Cancels Bail for Accused in Meghalaya Honeymoon Murder Case
excerpt: Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale set aside lower court orders, directing Sonam Raghuvanshi to surrender within three weeks for the alleged premeditated murder of her husband Raja Raghuvanshi.
body:
India's Supreme Court on Wednesday cancelled the bail of Sonam Raghuvanshi, the prime accused in the high-profile Meghalaya honeymoon murder case, ordering her to surrender to police within three weeks.

A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale set aside orders from both the Meghalaya High Court and a trial court that had granted Raghuvanshi bail on her fourth application. The court ruled that both lower courts committed an error in granting bail based on a technical defect in arrest documentation.

How the Case Unfolded

According to the prosecution, Raghuvanshi conspired with her alleged lover Raj Kushwaha and three hired assailants to murder her husband, Raja Raghuvanshi, during their honeymoon in Meghalaya. The couple married on May 12, 2025, and went missing after checking out of a homestay in Nongriat on May 23.

https://x.com/barandbench/status/2080181173444305303

Raja's body was recovered from a gorge near Weisawdong Falls on June 2, 2025. Sonam was traced and arrested near Ghazipur in Uttar Pradesh on June 9. The Meghalaya Police filed a chargesheet exceeding 700 pages alleging the murder was premeditated.

The Bail Dispute

After spending roughly 10 months in judicial custody at Shillong District Jail, Raghuvanshi was granted bail by a trial court on April 27 on her fourth application. The court found that arrest documents repeatedly cited Section 403(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — a non-existent provision — instead of Section 103(1), which deals with murder. The Meghalaya High Court upheld the order, questioning why the same error appeared across multiple official documents.

The State of Meghalaya, represented by Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, challenged the decision in the Supreme Court, arguing the citation was a typographical error that caused no prejudice to the accused.

Supreme Court Draws a Legal Line

The bench drew a critical distinction between complete non-service of arrest grounds and inadequate communication of reasons for arrest. "It is not as if the respondent was not served with the grounds of arrest," the court observed, according to LiveLaw. "There is a difference between non-service of grounds of arrest and not giving adequate reasons for arrest. While the first category would vitiate the arrest, in the second, one has to see the prejudice."

The court noted that Raghuvanshi had earlier expressed satisfaction with the reasons provided for her arrest, undermining her subsequent legal challenge on that ground.

"We are dealing with a case where the earlier orders rejecting bail on merits have attained finality. Trial has already begun. Continued enlargement of the respondent at this stage might hinder the ongoing trial."

— Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale, Supreme Court of India

The court also held that a defect in arrest documentation would not prevent the investigating agency from effecting a fresh arrest. "Law does not restrain the investigating agency from re-arresting a person," the bench observed.

Bench Flags Changing Family Dynamics

During the hearing, the bench and Solicitor General Mehta made broader observations about modern relationships and societal shifts in India. Mehta argued that the joint family system traditionally enabled elders to resolve disputes between couples, but the rise of nuclear families has led to increased separations and depression, according to NDTV.

Justice Sundresh responded: "Such incidents are bound to happen in a changing family system. We will see a rise in conflict with personal laws with the rise in matrimonial disputes. The present generation may be more knowledgeable than us, but in terms of dealing with pressure, they are more vulnerable."

Justice PB Varale added a pointed remark about digital misinformation: "Whatever is being shared on WhatsApp is being treated as knowledge."

What Comes Next

Raghuvanshi has three weeks to surrender before the Meghalaya Police. The court clarified that if the trial does not conclude within six months, she may file a fresh bail application. The case — State of Meghalaya v. Sonam Raghuvanshi (SLP (Crl.) No. 11944/2026) — will continue as the trial progresses in the lower court.

The ruling sets a significant precedent on how courts should evaluate claims of defective arrest documentation, distinguishing between procedural violations that invalidate an arrest and those that merely reflect administrative shortcomings.
